pharm: Third-generation cephalosporin (beta-lactam, bactericidal); cell-wall synthesis inhibitor
quick: Allergy, renal function, CBC, signs of CDAD
summary: Ceftizoxime is a parenteral (IV/IM) third-generation cephalosporin used for serious infections caused by susceptible Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms, including lower respiratory tract, urinary tract, intra-abdominal, skin, bone and joint infections, gonorrhea, pelvic inflammatory disease, septicemia and meningitis. It is bactericidal through inhibition of bacterial cell-wall synthesis and is stable to many beta-lactamases. It lacks a desacetyl metabolite and is largely excreted unchanged in urine, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. It is generally well tolerated, with hypersensitivity, transient hematologic and hepatic changes, and C. difficile colitis being the principal class concerns. The US brand (Cefizox) has been discontinued and the drug is not currently FDA-approved in the United States; this record draws on EMA/BNF/Martindale and the historical US prescribing information.
indications: Lower respiratory tract infections, including pneumonia

dosage.n: Continue at least 48-72 h after defervescence
Reserve highest doses for the most serious infections
Add antichlamydial cover if C. trachomatis suspected

admin: Reconstitute before IM or IV administration; inspect for particulates and discoloration
Give IV by slow injection over 3-5 minutes or by intermittent infusion over 30 minutes
For IM, inject deep into a large muscle mass; divide doses of 2 g between two sites
Obtain culture and susceptibility before starting therapy where possible
Continue treatment for at least 48-72 hours after the patient becomes afebrile or signs of infection resolve
Treat Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infections for a minimum of 10 days
moa: Ceftizoxime is a bactericidal beta-lactam that binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits the final transpeptidation step of bacterial cell-wall (peptidoglycan) synthesis. It is highly stable to many plasmid- and chromosomally mediated beta-lactamases, giving broad activity against Gram-negative bacilli. Unlike some related cephalosporins it has no microbiologically active metabolite.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to ceftizoxime, its excipients, or any cephalosporin
relative: Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity to penicillins or other beta-lactams (cross-reactivity risk) - use with caution
History of gastrointestinal disease, particularly colitis
monitor: Signs of allergic/anaphylactic reaction - discontinue and treat if they occur
Diarrhea suggestive of Clostridioides difficile colitis, which may appear during or after therapy
Renal function, especially with concurrent nephrotoxic drugs or in the elderly
Prolonged therapy: CBC, hematologic and hepatic parameters

preg: Animal reproduction studies have not shown evidence of impaired fertility or harm to the fetus, but there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Cephalosporins cross the placenta. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
lact: Ceftizoxime is excreted in human milk in low concentrations; exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman.
renal: Ceftizoxime is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidneys, so dose reduction is required in renal impairment. After an initial loading dose of 0.5-1 g, adjust maintenance dosing by creatinine clearance: for CrCl ~50-79 mL/min give 0.5-1.5 g every 8 hours; for CrCl ~5-49 mL/min give 0.25-1 g every 12 hours; and for CrCl 0-4 mL/min (including dialysis patients) give 0.5-1 g every 48 hours or 0.25-0.5 g every 24 hours. Use higher doses within each band for life-threatening infections. In hemodialysis patients, give a dose at the end of each dialysis session.
hepatic: No specific hepatic dose adjustment is required; transient elevations of AST, ALT, and alkaline phosphatase may occur.

moderate: Potent diuretics such as furosemide - possible additive nephrotoxicity
Probenecid - reduces renal tubular secretion and raises ceftizoxime plasma levels
interactions.food: Not applicable; ceftizoxime is administered parenterally.
interactions.alcohol: No disulfiram-like reaction reported (ceftizoxime lacks an N-methylthiotetrazole side chain).
interactions.diagnostics: May cause a positive direct Coombs test and a false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction (Benedict's/Fehling's/CLINITEST) methods; use enzyme-based glucose tests instead.

common: Injection-site reactions: pain, burning, induration (IM); phlebitis (IV)
Transient elevations of AST/ALT and alkaline phosphatase
emergency: Severe or persistent bloody diarrhea (possible C. difficile colitis)

monitoring: Assess for penicillin/cephalosporin/beta-lactam allergy before the first dose
Watch for hypersensitivity during and after administration
Renal function (BUN, creatinine), especially with nephrotoxic co-medications or in the elderly
Monitor for diarrhea / signs of C. difficile colitis
Prolonged therapy: periodic CBC and hepatic function
counsel: This antibiotic treats bacterial, not viral, infections such as the common cold
Complete the full prescribed course even if feeling better to avoid resistance and treatment failure
Report rash, itching, swelling, or trouble breathing immediately
Report watery or bloody diarrhea, even weeks after treatment
Tell your clinician about any prior allergic reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins, or other drugs
pk: IM ~1 h; end of IV infusion
Store dry powder 20-25 C, protect from light; use reconstituted solution per stability instructions
pearls: NOT FDA-approved / discontinued in the US (brand Cefizox withdrawn); this record is based on EMA/BNF/Martindale and the historical US prescribing information rather than a current openFDA label.
Eliminated largely unchanged by the kidneys with no active metabolite, so renal dose reduction is required (unlike ceftriaxone, which needs none for renal impairment alone).
Single 1 g IM dose treats uncomplicated gonorrhea; lacks activity against C. trachomatis, so add antichlamydial cover.
Lacks the N-methylthiotetrazole side chain, so no disulfiram reaction and no associated hypoprothrombinemic bleeding.
Usual 1-2 g q8-12h; escalate to 3-4 g q8h (up to ~12 g/day) for severe or life-threatening infections.
Removed by hemodialysis; give a supplemental dose at the end of each session.
missed: Parenteral, clinician-administered on a fixed schedule; if a scheduled dose is delayed, give it as soon as possible and adjust subsequent timing to maintain the prescribed interval rather than doubling up.
overdose: There is no specific antidote. Overdose may cause neurological effects, including seizures and encephalopathy, particularly in renal impairment where the drug accumulates. Discontinue the drug and provide supportive care; ceftizoxime is removed by hemodialysis, which may aid clearance in severe renal compromise or marked overdose.
